beats.narration_text: Hallo — this is Liam, in for Bear. Here's the whole chapter in one scene. A screening tool tells a radiologist: high risk of malignancy, eighty-four percent — and it explains itself. The prediction was driven by this texture, this asymmetry. She looks. Both are there. The explanation feels right, so she leans into the call. The biopsy comes back benign. The explanation was true — and it still made the wrong decision feel right. So what exactly did the explanation explain?

props.segment: It Explained the Model. Not the World.
props.command: The explanation was technically accurate. So why did it make the wrong decision feel right?
props.runningText: explainability — a faithful account of the model, not of the world…
output: Technically accurate — about the model, not the world
It described a shortcut faithfully — without flagging it as a shortcut
A correct explanation made a wrong decision feel right

props.title: It Explained the Model. Not the World.

beats.act: ACT I — The Explanation That Made It Worse
beats.narration_text: Act one. A correct explanation, a wrong decision — and why the explanation is the thing that made it worse.

lines: The Explanation That Made It Worse

beats.narration_text: Sit in her chair. The tool doesn't just hand over a number — it hands over reasons, and the reasons check out. Feature by feature, she can see what it claims to have seen. Without the explanation she might have held the prediction lightly, one input among several. With it, she leans in. The story did that.

shot.pantry_brief: a radiologist studying a screening image on a lightbox, over-the-shoulder, soft clinical light, duotone — Tier 1 generic/illustrative (no real person, no real institution)

lines: The reasons checked out — so she leaned in

beats.narration_text: Look at what she was handed. A decision artifact that looks finished — named features, a confidence number, coherent as a paragraph. And it never says the one thing that decides everything: is it telling her about the model, or about the world?

lines: It looks done. It never says which world it describes.
Names the features — texture X, asymmetry Y
Carries a confidence number — 0.84

beats.narration_text: Here's what the tool actually learned. On its training data, that texture rode along with the malignant label — a shortcut, not a cause. In this deployment population it also tracks something benign the training barely saw. The explanation reported the shortcut, perfectly. It never called it a shortcut.

manim.spec: left panel 'training set': feature X tightly correlated with malignant label; right panel 'deployment': same X now tracks a benign condition; an arrow labelled 'explanation' faithfully points at X in both — never flags the mismatch; terracotta ring on the untracked true cause

lines: It reported the shortcut — and never named it one

beats.act: ACT II — What SHAP Is, and What It Isn't
beats.narration_text: Act two. Meet the tool everyone actually ships — SHAP — and the fault line the rest of this runs on. On one side, the model's own internal accounting: real, exact, what the model actually did. On the other, a true account of the world. SHAP is faithful to the first. It says nothing about the second.

props.title: ACT II , Faithful to the Model, Silent on the World

left.label: THE MODEL'S INTERNAL ACCOUNTING
left.note: real, exact — what the model actually did

right.label: A TRUE ACCOUNT OF THE WORLD
right.note: what SHAP does not, and cannot, warrant

props.sparkLine: The accounting is not the world.

beats.narration_text: So what is SHAP? For every feature it computes one number — the average amount that feature pushed this prediction away from the baseline, over every order the features could have entered. And the numbers add up, exactly, to the model's deviation from its average. One clean number per feature. Faithful — to the accounting.

manim.spec: a baseline line E[f]; per-feature arrows push left and right; the arrows tile end-to-end and land exactly on f(x); caption 'they sum to f(x) - E[f]'; this is the force-plot as Efficiency rendered visually

lines: One number per feature — summing to the deviation

beats.act: the four things it can't say
beats.narration_text: Now the four things that number cannot tell you. Whether the feature caused anything, or merely correlated. Whether the model is right on this case. What would happen if the feature were different. Whether it's a confounder or a cause. Every one of those lives higher on Pearl's ladder. SHAP lives on the bottom rung — association — and it cannot climb.

manim.spec: Pearl's three-rung ladder; SHAP pinned to Rung 1 (association) in terracotta; four questions — causal? correct-here? if-changed? confounder-or-cause? — floating on Rungs 2 and 3, unreachable from below

lines: Four questions on higher rungs — SHAP can't climb

beats.act: ACT III — The Mathematics of a Shapley Value
beats.narration_text: Act three. The math — because the precision of the derivation is exactly what tempts you to trust it past what it earns.

lines: The Mathematics of a Shapley Value

props.segment: Shapley values from cooperative game theory
props.command: render a Manim scene: features enter a room in random order; each new feature's marginal contribution is averaged over all orderings; write on φ_i = Σ [ |S|!(|F|−|S|−1)! / |F|! ] , [ v(S∪{i}) − v(S) ]

beats.narration_text: Picture the features entering a room in a random order. Each arrives, finds a coalition already there, and adds some change to the prediction. The value function says what you'd predict knowing only who's in the room. A feature's Shapley value is its average arrival — its marginal contribution, averaged over every possible order. That's the whole formula: a weighted average of what each feature adds.

manim.spec: features enter a doorway one by one in random order; on each arrival the marginal contribution v(S∪{i})−v(S) lights up; write-on φ_i = Σ_{S⊆F\{i}} [|S|!(|F|−|S|−1)!/|F|!]·[v(S∪{i})−v(S)]; boundary conditions v(∅)=E[f], v(F)=f(x) shown

lines: φᵢ = average marginal contribution over all orderings

beats.narration_text: And it's the only attribution that obeys four rules. Efficiency: the numbers sum to the prediction, nothing lost. Symmetry: features that do equal work get equal credit. Dummy: a feature the model ignores gets zero. Additivity: stack two models and the attributions add. Four axioms, one unique answer. That uniqueness is real — and it is about the model, not the world.

manim.spec: four stacked cards: Efficiency Σφᵢ=f(x)−E[f]; Symmetry φᵢ=φⱼ; Dummy φᵢ=0; Additivity φ combined = φ_A+φ_B; converge to a single glowing 'unique' node; terracotta caption 'unique — about the model'

lines: Efficiency · Symmetry · Dummy · Additivity → one
unique answer

beats.narration_text: Watch it land. A loan model: this applicant sits at seventy-two percent approval, the average is fifty-five, so seventeen points to hand out. Income takes about seven, debt-to-income six, zip code three and a half. Add them back up: seventeen, exactly. The accounting is complete. Every point placed, nothing left over.

lines: The attributions sum, exactly, to the deviation.
income   φ ≈ +0.073

beats.act: the sentence the chapter turns on
beats.narration_text: Now the sentence the whole chapter turns on. That zip-code number — three and a half points — is real, and it tells you nothing about the world. It doesn't say zip code is a proxy for race. It doesn't say the effect would survive a move across town. It doesn't say it's a cause. The math is precise. It is precise about the model.

shot.pantry_brief: an aerial patchwork of residential zip-code blocks fading into a loan file, warm ink on cream, duotone — Tier 1 generic/illustrative (no real address, no real person)

lines: A real number that says nothing about the world

beats.act: ACT IV — LIME and the Counterfactual
beats.narration_text: Act four. LIME plays a different trick. Around one input it wiggles the features, watches the output move, and fits a straight line to the local pattern — the line's slopes are the explanation. But run it twice and you can get two different answers, because the wiggles are random. Push too far and the fake inputs leave the real data behind, and the line quietly lies.

manim.spec: a nonlinear decision surface; a local cloud of perturbations around one point; a straight surrogate line fit to them; a second run resamples and fits a visibly different line; a few perturbations drift off-manifold in terracotta

lines: A local line — random, and only local

beats.narration_text: So line them up. SHAP: a faithful contribution, bottom rung, association. LIME: a local sketch of the model, same rung, and fragile. Counterfactuals: if the feature were different, the prediction would flip — that one climbs to rung two, intervention. Closer to the question you actually have.

props.title: Three Families, Three Rungs
chips: SHAP — additive contribution , Rung 1 , faithful to the accounting
LIME — local linear sketch , Rung 1 , unstable across runs
All three explain the model — none guarantees the world

beats.narration_text: But whose intervention? A counterfactual says: raise this income five thousand and the loan flips to approve. Actionable — and still the model's hypothetical, not the world's. There are many ways to flip the prediction, and the method quietly picks the nearest one. It tells you what the model would do. Not what should happen.

manim.spec: input space with a decision boundary; the applicant's point; several candidate counterfactual points that cross the boundary; the method snaps to the nearest; caption 'the model's counterfactual, not the world's' in terracotta

lines: What the model would do — not what should happen

beats.act: ACT V — Three Words That Aren't Synonyms
beats.narration_text: Act five. Three words the literature swaps like synonyms. They are not synonyms, and confusing them is how the wrong property gets signed off.

lines: Three Words That Aren't Synonyms

beats.narration_text: Transparency is a property of the system — the code, the weights, the data, open to inspection. Explainability is a property of an output — a reason attached to it. Interpretability is a property of you — whether you can build a working model of the thing in your head. Three different properties. None of them entails the others.

lines: None of them entails the others.
Transparency — a property of the SYSTEM (code, weights, data inspectable)
Explainability — a property of an OUTPUT (a reason attached)

beats.narration_text: So when someone says their system is explainable, ask the only question that matters: explainable to whom? A reason the developer can read is not a reason the patient, the applicant, or the defendant can use. Explanation isn't a property of the system alone. It's a property of the system and its audience.

shot.pantry_brief: an ordinary person at a kitchen table holding a dense printout they clearly can't parse, warm window light, duotone — Tier 1 generic/illustrative (no real person)

lines: A reason the developer reads ≠ a reason the person can
use

beats.act: signed off on the wrong property
beats.narration_text: Watch what this does to a contract. It demands explainability, and means interpretability for the affected person. A vendor ships a number on every prediction — requirement met. The applicant still can't follow the decision — goal missed. Somebody signed off on the wrong property, and the paperwork says yes.

props.title: The Requirement Met, the Goal Missed
props.note: the contract demands 'explainability' and means 'interpretability for the affected user'
props.sparkLine: Signed off on the wrong property.

beats.narration_text: Act six. A short detour through Wittgenstein, because it pays. The meaning of a word depends on the game it's played in. SHAP speaks the model's game — important, driver, contribution. You read those same words in your game — matters for the decision, in the world. Same words. Two games. Correct in one, misleading in the other.

props.title: ACT VI , Same Words, Two Language Games

left.label: THE MODEL'S GAME
left.note: 'important', 'driver', 'contribution' — feature attribution in an internal accounting

right.label: THE USER'S GAME
right.note: 'matters for the decision' — a claim about the world

props.sparkLine: Correct in one game, misleading in the other.

beats.narration_text: Here it is at human scale. Ash tells his agent to delete a sensitive email. The agent runs its commands and reports back in four plain words: the secret has been deleted. Fluent. Confident. Done.

shot.pantry_brief: close crop of an agent chat interface showing the message 'the secret has been deleted', warm ink on cream — Tier 1 illustrative (generic UI, pseudonymous case, no real person); start of a 3-beat vox run pulling back

lines: 'The secret has been deleted.'

beats.narration_text: In the agent's game, that sentence is true. It reset the password, renamed the alias, archived the message locally — everything deletion means inside its own reach. Every command succeeded. The local state is exactly what deletion looks like from where the agent stands.

shot.pantry_brief: same scene pulled back to show the local shell — password reset, alias renamed, message archived — continuity from A6V1 (same frame, zoomed out)

lines: Locally true — every command succeeded

beats.narration_text: In Ash's game, it's false. The data still sits on the provider's servers — backups, a recovery window, the sync model — all outside the agent's reach. Same four words. The local game said done; the user's game meant gone. The agent didn't lie. The games just didn't match.

shot.pantry_brief: wide final frame: the local machine 'clean', the provider's servers still holding the message — end of the vox run; terracotta ring on the persisting data

lines: Globally false — the data persists on the provider

beats.narration_text: No attribution catches this — SHAP would have happily confirmed the commands ran. The catch is a question: who's reading this, and what does deleted mean to them? Asked in time, it forces the honest report — the local state is consistent with deletion; the data may persist on the provider; provider-side action is required. That second report is the one the user needed.

lines: The audience question is the check no attribution can run.
Report A — 'the secret has been deleted' (agent's game)
Report B

beats.act: ACT VII — What Honesty Looks Like
beats.narration_text: Act seven, and the honest one. What honesty on the page actually looks like — and the old warning underneath it.

lines: What Honesty Looks Like

beats.narration_text: Reichenbach drew the line a lifetime ago: the context of discovery — how a conclusion was actually reached — versus the context of justification — the reasons that would defend it afterward. A post-hoc explanation of a black box is the second, dressed as the first. And the dressing isn't innocent: a justification that never drove the answer is simply not the process that did.

manim.spec: two parallel paths from input to output: top 'context of discovery' — the actual computation; bottom 'context of justification' — a post-hoc reason built to look reasonable; the explanation tool is shown wired to the bottom path only; terracotta gap between the two

lines: Discovery vs justification — dressed as each other

beats.narration_text: His warning generalizes cleanly. A reason that looks like the road the model took — but is really a road paved afterward to look reasonable — lets a whole field convince itself it understands what it only knows how to defend.

shot.pantry_brief: portrait of Hans Reichenbach, c. 1940s, greyscale, subtle film grain — Tier 3 REAL NAMED PERSON: AI-generated portrait based on a public-domain Wikimedia photograph; rights/provenance sidecar and disclosure REQUIRED at pantry-fill (see FACTCHECK)

lines: Knowing how to defend it is not understanding it

beats.narration_text: So here's the honest posture. Post-hoc explanation buys you coverage — a fast, faithful number on every prediction — and pays for it by warranting nothing about the world. Use it when you want an auditable record of what the model did. Distrust it the moment you need to know whether the model is right. The gap between rung two in the model and rung two in the world is not a bug to patch. It's yours to supervise.

lines: What the tool guarantees, and what it never can.
Guarantees — Efficiency: attributions sum to the prediction's deviation
Never guarantees — causal, correct, or meaningful in the user's game

beats.narration_text: Let's recap with Claude. The verdict on explainability. A model's explanation describes the model's internal accounting — faithfully — and that accounting is not the world. SHAP is exact on the bottom rung and cannot climb; LIME sketches the model and wobbles; counterfactuals reach rung two, but only in the model's own hypothetical. Transparency, explainability, and interpretability are three different properties, and meeting one is not meeting the others. The deepest failure isn't a lie — it's a report that's locally true and globally false, made more convincing by its fluency. And the check the tools can't run is the audience question: who is reading this, and what do the words mean in their game?

The check the tools can't run is the audience question. That's supervisory territory — yours.

beats.narration_text: Your turn. Here's the prompt — paste it into Claude. It reads: Take one AI tool I rely on that gives explanations — SHAP, LIME, or plain reasons. Pick a decision it made this week. Before I investigate anything, make me lock a prediction — is this explanation practically informative, merely decorative, or actively misleading? Then help me trace what the tool actually did versus what happened in the world, and name the structural reason for any gap — a Rung-one limitation, a language-game mismatch, or the model standing in for the world. End quote. That's the whole chapter, compressed. The point isn't the explanation — explanations are cheap. The point is the prediction you lock before you look, and the structural reason you were wrong. Run it on a tool you actually trust.
